Let me talk through why the held out set matters more than the training set at this point, because I keep having to re-explain it to myself. The training data is already past the steep part of the curve, so another thousand rows would move the model by a couple of points at best. The problem is that a couple of points is exactly the size of change I currently cannot see. With eighty odd cases, only a very large improvement shows up as anything other than noise, which means every small win and every small regression looks identical from where I am sitting. That is a bad position to be in when the whole plan is to run a series of short experiments and keep the ones that helped, because I would be choosing between configurations on the basis of coin flips and then writing the coin flips down as findings. So the order is: finish the measuring instrument, check that it disagrees with me sometimes, and only then start spending money on runs. The other thing I want to hold onto is that the two numbers stay separate. A model that copies its input scores about half on a blended figure and looks mediocre rather than broken, and a model that edits everything scores badly in a way that is obvious immediately. One number hides the first failure and not the second, so there is no version of this where a single accuracy figure is the thing I report.

Alright so this is the whole thing about the export step, and I want to say it once so I stop worrying about it. The way it works is that the training library gives you an adapter, which is a small set of extra weights sitting beside the frozen base, and the thing I actually ship is a single file that the runtime can load on a laptop without any Python at all. Those two are not the same object, and the conversion between them is where I expect this to break. The failure I am afraid of is not a crash, a crash would be a gift. The failure is a file that loads perfectly, reports no error anywhere, and then produces exactly the same output as the base model did, because the adapter was silently dropped somewhere in the merge. Nothing warns you about that. The score just comes back looking like the fine-tune did nothing, and then I spend two days blaming the data. So the rule is that every converted file gets checked against one input where the base model is known to be wrong, before anything else happens with it, and that check goes in the log with the run rather than in my head.

Right, I am writing down the brisket properly this time because every cook does it differently and last week it came out grey. This is the one we put on when the market has the cheap end cuts, not the braise on the menu, and the difference is that this one gets a dry rub the night before and the menu one does not. Buy the whole piece with the fat cap on, and do not let them trim it for you, because they always take too much and then it dries out in the second hour. What goes in the rub? Coarse salt. Black pepper, cracked, not ground. Brown sugar. Smoked paprika. Ground fennel. The proportions are not fussy but the salt has to be more than you think, roughly a heaped tablespoon for a piece that size, and the sugar is there for colour more than sweetness, so if it looks like a lot it probably is not. You rub it the night before and you leave it uncovered on a tray in the cold room because the surface needs to dry out, and if you cover it you get a wet skin and no crust. Then in the morning you take it out an hour before it goes in the oven, and you do not rinse it. People always want to rinse it and it undoes the whole point. The oven goes low, and I mean genuinely low, and then you leave it alone for the first three hours, and after that you start looking at it every forty minutes or so. When the fat has gone soft and the thin end feels loose, you put the foil on and you keep going until the middle gives way when you push a spoon into it. If it stalls, and it will stall, that is normal and it is not the oven, so do not turn the heat up because you will tighten the meat and you will not get it back. The resting is the part everybody rushes. It needs a full hour out of the oven, loosely covered, somewhere out of a draught, and it will not go cold in that time. If you slice it early, all the liquid runs out onto the board and the pieces fall apart in the pass. Slice it against the grain and slice it thicker than you would for the menu one because the fibres are shorter after this long a cook and thin slices just collapse. The sauce is whatever is in the tray, poured off, left to settle for ten minutes, and then the fat lifted off the top, and it needs nothing else in it. If the tray has caught, and only if it has caught, put a little of the stock in and scrape it while it is still hot, but taste it first because caught sugar turns bitter quickly and you cannot take that back out. And write on the card that this one needs starting two days before service, not one, because the rub night is not optional and every time somebody has tried to shortcut it we have ended up serving something that tastes fine and looks wrong, and then I get asked why it is not the same as last month.

So the thing I keep failing to explain in the meeting is that the queue is not the problem, the queue is only where the problem becomes visible. There are a few things going on at once and they interact with each other, which is why every fix we have tried so far has moved the symptom somewhere else instead of removing it. The producers batch on a timer, the consumers batch on a count, and the timer is shorter than the time it takes to fill a batch, so under light load we send tiny batches and under heavy load we send enormous ones and neither path is the one anybody actually tuned. On top of that the retry policy is per message rather than per batch, so a single poisoned message can take a whole batch down with it and then the redelivery arrives while the original batch is still in flight. I do not want to write a proposal that says fix the batching, because we have said that twice already and both times somebody changed a constant and declared victory. What I want to write is a description of the interaction that is detailed enough that the next person cannot fix one half of it and walk away feeling good. The measurement part matters more than the fix, honestly. If we cannot see the batch size distribution over a whole day then we are going to have this same argument again in April with different numbers, and I am not doing that again.

Right, this is the order I want to do the queue work in, and I want it written down this time because last time I described it in a paragraph and two people picked different starting points out of it. Before anything gets changed. First land the metric for batch size and hold it for a week. Second move the retry policy from per message to per batch. Third make the two batching triggers agree on a single unit. The reason the metric goes first is not process for the sake of process, it is that we have no idea what the distribution looks like under real load and every number anybody has quoted in the last month came off a staging box with synthetic traffic on it. The retry change goes second because it is the only one of the three that is safe to ship on its own, and it removes the redelivery interference that makes the batching behaviour impossible to read. The unit change goes last because it is the one that will need a rollback plan, and I would much rather have a full week of clean measurement before anybody touches it. If somebody wants to argue about that order I would rather they argue now, in writing, than change it quietly halfway through the sprint. Okay, this is the write up for the collector change and it is going to be longer than usual because the reviewer is probably going to be somebody who has never touched this service. The symptom is that the dashboard shows gaps of between forty seconds and two minutes, always on the hour, and always on the hosts that carry the most traffic. Support has three tickets about it and two of them are from the same customer, who noticed that their alert did not fire during a real outage, which is why I am not treating this as cosmetic. What is actually happening is that the collector rotates its output file on the hour and it does the rotation on the same thread that accepts writes, so while the rotation is in progress the accept path blocks, and on a busy host the rotation takes long enough that the upstream buffer fills and starts dropping. On a quiet host it finishes in under a second and nobody sees anything, which is why this never reproduced in staging and why we spent two weeks blaming the network. The change does three things and I want them read in this order. First it moves the rotation onto its own thread so the accept path never waits on file system work. Second it makes the buffer drop policy explicit and counted so that a drop is visible instead of being inferred from a hole in a graph. Third it adds a metric for rotation duration, because I do not want the next person to have to reconstruct this from timestamps the way I did. Testing was mostly load based rather than unit based and I would rather say that plainly than dress it up. I ran the collector under synthetic load at roughly three times the peak rate we see on the busiest host, for six hours, with rotation forced every five minutes instead of hourly, and there were no gaps and no drops at all. I also ran the same shape of test against the old build to confirm that it fails the way I claim it fails, and it does, reliably, inside the first two rotations. There are unit tests for the drop counter and for the rotation duration metric, but there is no unit test for the threading change itself, because I could not write one that would fail for the right reason rather than by luck. What I have not done is test any of this on the ARM hosts, because I do not have access to them, and somebody who does should run it there before this goes past canary. I also have not touched the reader side at all, so if there are historical gaps already written into old files then this does nothing about those, and the support tickets will need a separate answer about the data we have already lost. Rollback is a config flag and it is off by default in this branch, which I know is backwards, so tell me if you want that flipped before it merges.

I want to get this out of my head before the review because I am going to be the person arguing against the change and I would rather have thought about it properly than just react in the meeting. The proposal is to rename everything in the storage layer so that the field names match the API, which in practice means the database goes from snake case to camel case across about forty tables. I understand why it is being proposed. Every new person who joins spends their first fortnight writing a mapping in their head, and there are three places in the codebase where somebody got it wrong and the bug was invisible until a customer noticed, so the cost is real and it is not only aesthetics. My problem is the size of the blast radius against the size of the benefit. The database is not the only consumer. There are two reporting jobs that were written before I joined and neither of them goes through the ORM, they read the tables directly with hand written SQL, and the person who wrote them left in twenty twenty three. There is also the export that the finance team runs at month end, which produces a file whose headers are the raw column names, and somebody downstream of us has a spreadsheet with formulas that reference those headers both by position and by name. I know that is fragile and I know it is not our problem in theory, but the last time we changed a header we found out about it eleven days later from a very unhappy email. If we are going to do this then I think it has to be done as a view layer first, so the old names keep working while the new ones exist, and then we remove the old names in a separate change once we can prove nobody is reading them. That is more work and it is less satisfying, but it is the only version of this that I would sign off on. What I do not want is the version where we rename the columns, fix everything that breaks in the test suite, ship it, and then spend a month finding the things the test suite cannot see. The other thing I keep coming back to is that camel case in the database does not actually solve the mapping problem, it moves it, because the API is not the only interface we have. The event stream uses kebab case for topic names and screaming snake case for the header keys, and nobody is proposing to change those, so a new person still has three conventions to hold in their head instead of two. If the goal is to reduce the number of conventions then the honest version of this proposal is much bigger than the storage layer, and if the goal is only to make the ORM mapping file shorter then we should say that out loud and weigh it against a month of migration risk. Either way I am not against it in principle, I am against doing it in one step.

Before I sign the report I want to talk through the tolerance question, because the number the customer has written into the order is tighter than the number on our own drawing and nobody had noticed until this morning. The order says the bore is to be held to two hundredths of a millimetre. Our drawing says five hundredths. On this machine, with this fixture, we can hold five reliably and we can hold three on a good day with a fresh tool, but two is less than the repeatability of the machine, so what would actually happen is that we would make the parts, measure them, sort them, and the customer would be paying for sorting rather than for accuracy. That is a legitimate thing to sell if it is what they want, but it has to be agreed and it has to be priced, and at the moment it is neither. The second thing is the surface finish. The order does not specify one at all, which usually means whatever falls out of the process is acceptable, but this part runs against a seal, and if it is rougher than about one and a half micrometres the seal will not last a season. I would rather write a number onto the drawing now and have the argument than deliver a part that meets every stated requirement and then fails in service. My proposal is that we quote the five hundredths as standard, quote the three as an option with the sorting cost inside it, and put a finish requirement on the drawing with our own number on it. If they say no to all three then at least the file shows that we asked.

This is the handover for the reporting models and I am dictating it into the readme, so keep every bracket exactly where I put it because half of this is literal text that people copy. The models are templated, which means the file you open is not the query that runs. Anywhere you see {{ ref('stg_orders') }} that resolves to the schema for whichever target you are on, so in development it is my personal schema and in production it is the analytics schema, and the single most common mistake is hardcoding the production name into a model because it worked once in a notebook. The date filter is {{ var('start_date') }} and it has a default in the project file, which means a model can run and be silently wrong for six months if somebody forgets to pass the variable, and that is exactly what happened to the refunds model in April. The incremental block matters. It is {% if is_incremental() %} then the where clause then {% endif %}, and the percent signs are part of the syntax, they are not a typo and they are not a comment marker. If you delete the endif the compile error points at the bottom of the file rather than at the block, which sends people looking in the wrong place for an hour. There is one macro I wrote that you should know about. It takes a column and a grain and returns a truncated date, and it is called safe_trunc, and it exists because the warehouse function throws on nulls rather than passing them through. Do not replace it with the built in until you have checked the null behaviour in the current version, because I checked it twice and it changed between versions. On the naming, staging models are stg_ then the source system, intermediate models are int_ then the entity, and marts are just the business name with no prefix. I did not invent that, it is the convention from the framework docs, and I mention it because two people have already asked me whether they can use a different prefix for their team. They cannot. On testing, every model has at least a not_null and a unique test on its key, and those live in the yml file beside the model rather than in the sql, and the yml is whitespace sensitive so if a test disappears without an error the indentation is the first thing to check. When a test fails the compiled sql for that test is written into the target folder, and reading that file is much faster than reasoning about the test definition. One warning about the docs site. If you put a colon inside a description without quoting the whole string, the yml parses but the description comes out truncated at the colon, and there is no error anywhere. I lost most of an afternoon to that. Finally, the orchestration. The daily run is a single command with a selector, and the selector syntax uses a plus sign to mean downstream, so the argument is the model name followed immediately by a plus with no space, and if you put a space in the shell splits it and the run does nothing quietly.

Long note on the stock reconciliation, because I have been asked for it twice and I want one version of it that I can point at. The headline is that the system count and the physical count disagree by about four per cent by value, and almost none of that four per cent is theft, which is what everybody assumes when they hear a variance number. Start with what the four per cent is made of. Just over half of it is the returns process. A return is booked back into stock at the moment the label is scanned at the depot, but the item does not become sellable until somebody inspects it, and the gap between those two events averages nine days. So for nine days the system believes we have an item that we cannot sell, and if the count happens in those nine days the item is present, sellable in the system, and physically sitting in a cage waiting for a decision. Second piece is the multipack problem. Some products are sold both singly and in packs of six, and the pack is a separate code that decrements six of the single code when it ships. If somebody breaks a pack on the shop floor and sells the units individually, which happens because customers ask, then the single code goes negative and the pack code stays high, and the two errors are the same size and opposite sign so they cancel in the total and both show up in the by line detail. That is why the summary looks better than the detail, and anybody who has only ever seen the summary thinks the detail is broken. Third piece, and this is the smallest but the one that generates the most email, is the transfers. A transfer between the two sites is a single transaction in the system and two events in reality, and if the receiving site does not confirm on the same day then for a period the stock exists in neither place. Over a month there are maybe forty of those and each one is small. What I want to change. The returns booking should happen at inspection and not at scan, which is a configuration change rather than a project, and on its own it takes the variance from four per cent to under two. The multipack thing needs a rule that a pack cannot be broken without a transaction, and that is a training problem more than a systems one. The transfers I would leave alone for now because the effort is high and the amount is trivial. One thing I want to be careful about in how this gets presented. If I put a four per cent variance in a slide with no explanation, somebody senior reads shrinkage and the next question is about security cameras, and then we spend money on the wrong thing entirely. So I would rather present the three pieces first and the total last. I have put the working in the where house folder with the queries beside it so anybody can re run the numbers themselves rather than taking my word for it.

This is the shape of the event store proposal and I am going to talk through all of it before I write any of it down properly. The core of it is that we stop treating the audit log as a table people query and start treating it as a stream that things subscribe to, and the first consequence of that is that we keep the retention at thirty days in the hot store and everything older goes to object storage in daily files. The reason is not cost, although cost is nice, the reason is that every incident where the audit table has hurt us has been a query pattern nobody predicted, and a table invites those queries in a way that a set of daily files does not. Second piece, the writers. Right now there are four services writing into that table directly, and two of them do it inside the same transaction as the business change, which is why we have had two incidents where an audit insert failure rolled back a customer action. In the new shape nobody writes directly. Everything goes through one small library that appends to the stream, and the library is deliberately boring, no batching, no retries beyond the local buffer, and a hard rule that a failure to append never propagates back into the caller's transaction. If we lose an audit event because the buffer filled, that is a worse outcome than a lost event today, and I want that written down as an accepted tradeoff rather than discovered later by somebody reading the code. Third piece, the readers, and this is where I expect the argument. The reports team want to keep their existing queries working, which means we need a view that looks like the old table, and I am willing to build that view but only for the hot window. If you want to ask a question about last year you are going to read the daily files, and you are going to do it with the tool the data team already uses rather than a new endpoint we maintain forever. Fourth piece, the schema, and my position is that the payload stays opaque. We record who, what, when, and a blob, and we do not try to normalise the blob into columns, because every attempt to do that here has ended with forty nullable columns and a migration nobody wants to run. Validation happens at write time in the library, against a schema the owning team publishes, and if the schema changes the old events keep the old shape forever. Last piece, the migration itself, which is the boring part and the part that will take the longest. We dual write for two weeks, then we cut the readers over one at a time, then we stop writing to the table but leave it in place for another month before anybody is allowed to drop it. The rollback story at every step is that we turn the dual write back on, which is why the dual write period matters more than it looks on the diagram. Sorry, not thirty days for the hot retention, it has to be ninety days, thirty was the number in the old proposal and the compliance review moved it before Christmas.

Postmortem notes for the Thursday outage, spoken not written, I will file it properly tomorrow. Impact first. Card payments failed for eleven minutes for customers whose session landed on the new cluster, which is about a fifth of traffic in that window, and everything else was fine throughout, which is why the top level dashboard looked green for the first six minutes. Detection was a customer email before it was an alert, and that is the finding I care most about. Sequence. On Wednesday evening we finished the Kubernetties upgrade on the new cluster, which had been staged for three weeks and had gone through staging twice without incident. The upgrade changed the default value of one probe timeout from one second to two hundred milliseconds. Our payments service has a readiness check that talks to the token cache, and the token cache is in another region for reasons that made sense when it was built and make no sense now, so that check takes between one hundred and eight hundred milliseconds depending on how the network feels. Under the old default it always passed. Under the new default it passed most of the time, which is worse, because a probe that fails all the time takes a service out and a probe that fails a third of the time makes the service flap. Pods went unready, traffic shifted to the pods that were still ready, those pods took more load, their own checks got slower, and about four minutes into that spiral we had no ready pods in that cluster at all. The load balancer kept sending traffic because its own health check hits a different path that does not touch the cache. Recovery. Somebody sensible raised the timeout back to one second in the chart values and rolled the deployment, and that was the whole fix, eleven minutes end to end from the first customer email. We did not roll the upgrade back and I do not think we should have. What I want to come out of this. First, the readiness check should not talk to the cache at all, because a readiness check that depends on another region is not a readiness check, it is a distributed system with a boolean output. Second, we need to read the changed defaults in a release rather than the headline features, and I am not going to pretend that is a process fix, it is a habit and habits need a person not a document. Third, the dashboard that looked green needs a per cluster row, because the aggregate view is exactly the view that hides a partial outage. Fourth, and this is the uncomfortable one, staging passed twice because staging has the cache in the same region, so staging cannot ever have caught this. That is worth more than the other three put together and it is also the most expensive to fix, so I expect it to be the one that does not happen. Blame section, deliberately short. The person who ran the upgrade did everything the runbook asked for and the runbook was wrong.

Reading notes on the transcription stack, mostly for myself, I will turn this into a proper summary later. The starting point is that the recogniser and the cleanup model are two different problems and the literature keeps treating them as one. Parakeet, the one we actually run, already does punctuation and capitalisation and it does number formatting better than I expected, so the residual is much smaller than the papers assume. When I fed it the deposit sentence with a spoken figure and a spoken time it came back with the currency symbol and the clock time correct and the filler removed, which means every paper that measures cleanup by punctuation restoration is measuring something our pipeline has already solved. What is left over is a completely different shape of problem. It is retraction, where the speaker says a number and then changes it. It is words that were transcribed correctly and are still wrong, because the recogniser had no way to know the domain. It is layout that comes from how somebody spoke rather than from a formatting instruction. None of those are measured by word error rate at all, which is the second thing I keep running into, because every benchmark in the area reports word error rate and word error rate is blind to a fluent wrong answer. A model that turns a hesitant sentence into a confident different sentence can score better while being worse. On sizes, the interesting result is that the small end holds up much better than the scaling story predicts, and the reason seems to be that this task is narrow, the output is mostly a copy of the input, and the hard part is knowing when not to act rather than knowing how to write. There is a fine tune of a six hundred million parameter base that reports token accuracy in the mid nineties on held out cases, and there is a three hundred and fifty million one shipping inside a product on a laptop, so the practical floor is far lower than a two billion parameter model. The failure mode at every size is the same and it is overcorrection, which is why the training set needs as many rows that ask for nothing as rows that ask for a change. On the recogniser side specifically, para keet drifts on proper nouns in a way that is very consistent, it substitutes the most probable in vocabulary sequence, so a tool name becomes two ordinary English words rather than a misspelling, and that is actually good news because two ordinary words in a technical sentence are detectable from context. What is not detectable is a person's name, and I have not found any paper that solves that without a vocabulary list supplied at run time. Last note to myself, when Pair a keet loses the final word of a clip the transcript ends in a comma rather than a full stop, and that trailing comma is the only signal that the clip was cut, so whatever we build must not tidy it away.

Notes towards the referee report, and I will decide at the end whether any of this goes in the letter or stays in my own file. The paper is careful and the experiment is real, and I want to say that first because most of what follows is criticism and criticism reads harsher in a list than it does in a conversation. The central claim is that the intervention improves retention, and the evidence for it is a difference of four percentage points in a single cohort. My problem is not the size of the effect, which is plausible, it is that the cohort is the same cohort in which the intervention was designed, and the authors are the instructors of record. That is not a fatal objection and I am not going to pretend it is, but it belongs in the limitations section rather than in a footnote on page eleven where it currently sits. The second issue is the comparison group, which is the previous year, and the previous year is the year the timetable changed. Anybody who has taught through a timetable change knows that attendance patterns move for reasons that have nothing to do with pedagogy, and the paper does not mention the change at all. I do not think the authors are hiding it. I think they did not notice, because the people who notice a timetable change are the people who administer it. The third issue is smaller and easier to fix. The instrument they use to measure engagement has four items and they report a single composite score, and one of those four items is about whether the student found the material interesting, which is not engagement, it is satisfaction, and mixing the two is how this literature ended up with twenty measures that correlate with each other and with nothing else. Dropping that item would strengthen the result rather than weakening it, which is worth saying explicitly because authors hear any request to drop data as an attack. What I want to recommend is a revision rather than a rejection, and I want the revision to be substantive rather than cosmetic. The honest version of this paper is a description of a promising intervention in one setting with an acknowledged confound, and that paper is publishable and useful. The version currently submitted claims to have measured something general, and it has not, and the gap between those two papers is about four paragraphs of writing rather than a year of new work. Working through the restructure of the reference section before I write any of it, and this is thinking aloud rather than a plan anybody should act on yet. The problem with the current reference is not that it is wrong, it is that it is organised the way the code is organised rather than the way a reader arrives. Everything lives under the module that implements it, which is perfect if you already know which module you need and useless otherwise, and the search log says most people arrive with a task rather than a module name. The top three searches last month were about authentication tokens, about rate limits, and about retrying a failed request, and none of those three is a module. So the shape I want is a task oriented reference on top of the generated one, not instead of it. The generated pages stay exactly as they are, because they are complete and they are accurate and they cost nothing to maintain, and I have watched two previous attempts at a handwritten reference rot within a release. What I add is a layer of task pages that link into the generated pages, and the rule for a task page is that it answers one question, contains at least one complete runnable example, and never explains a concept that has its own page. The token page is the one I want to write first because it is the one people get wrong, and they get it wrong in a specific way. They read that a token expires in an hour, they write a refresh loop on a timer, and then the loop and the clock drift apart under load and they see authentication failures that look random. The correct pattern is to refresh on a failure rather than on a schedule, and that pattern is currently documented in a sentence in the middle of the errors page. Rate limits are the second one and the issue there is that we document the limit but not the header that tells you how much of it you have left, so everybody implements a fixed delay and the fixed delay is either too slow or too aggressive. Retries are the third and that page does not exist at all, which is an embarrassment given the number of support tickets that end with somebody being told to add a backoff. On the examples themselves, every one has to run against the sandbox with no edits beyond a key, and I want them tested in the pipeline rather than reviewed by eye, because an example that no longer compiles is worse than no example, it costs the reader twenty minutes and it costs us their trust. That means the examples live in the repository as real files and get pulled into the page at build time rather than being pasted into the text, which is a build change and needs somebody who is not me to agree to it. Last thing, migration. Nothing gets deleted and no address changes in the first pass. The task pages are additive, they go in the navigation above the generated section, and if the search log in three months says people are still landing on the generated pages first then the experiment failed and we have lost nothing but my time.

Okay, this is the test report for the release candidate and I am dictating it because I want it in the channel before the standup and typing it will take too long. Overall position first. The one real failure is in the payment retry flow. The case is the one where the first attempt times out and the second attempt succeeds, and what should happen is that the order ends up in one state with one charge. What actually happens, about one time in six, is that the order shows two charge records, both for the correct amount, one of them marked void. I have tried tightening the timeout, I have tried running it on the slower machine, and I have tried it with the network shaped to add half a second, and all three of those make it fail more often but none of them make it fail every time. That is what makes me think it is a race in the writer and not a logic error in the retry decision, because a logic error would be deterministic. On coverage, the areas I have not touched at all are the reporting screens and the admin import, because neither changed in this release and both take an hour to walk through manually. If somebody tells me a shared library under them changed then I will do it, but on what I can see in the diff they are untouched. The error message on an expired session now says the session is invalid rather than expired, which is technically true and will generate support tickets. So my recommendation, given the money is correct and the record is not, is that I would rather we del- delay the tag by a day and let the writer race be understood than ship it and explain two charge rows to finance at the end of the month.

This is the case summary for the escalation on the retail customer, and I am dictating it so the next shift has the whole story in one place instead of reading forty comments in reverse order. The customer reported that their point of sale terminals were dropping the connection to our service for a few seconds at a time, several times an hour, always in the afternoon and never in the morning. First contact was Tuesday and the first thing I did was the thing we always do, which is ask them to reproduce it with the diagnostic build so we get timestamps we can trust, and to their credit they did that within a day. What came back was interesting. The drops are real, they are between four and nine seconds, and they line up almost exactly with a scheduled job on their side that pushes the price file. The price file is about eleven megabytes and it goes out over the same link the terminals use, and the link is not as fat as the customer believes it is, because I asked them for the circuit details and what they have is not what they are paying for. So my working theory by Wednesday was that this is congestion on their side and not a fault in our service at all. Then it got complicated. They pushed the price file at a quiet hour as a test, deliberately, and the terminals dropped anyway, which killed my theory in one message. So I went back to the timestamps and looked at what else is common to the afternoon, and the answer is the number of terminals actually transacting, which roughly triples after two o'clock. When I plotted drops against concurrent sessions rather than against time of day, the relationship is much cleaner, and there is a step at about forty concurrent sessions where the drops start. Forty is not a number that should mean anything, but it is very close to a connection pool limit in the version of the client library they are running, which is two majors behind. I have not proved that yet. What would prove it is either a packet capture at the moment of a drop, which they are nervous about because of card data, or a test with the current library on a single site, which they can do and which I have asked for. My recommendation for the next shift is to keep pushing gently for the single site upgrade test and to resist the urge to blame their circuit in writing, because the quiet hour test already showed the circuit is not the whole story and if we put it in a formal note we will have to walk it back. Also please do not close the parent case even if the child cases go quiet, because this customer measures us on the parent case and closing it early reads as us declaring victory. The account manager has a call with them Friday morning and wants a one line status, and the honest one line is that we have a strong lead, a limited scope test requested, and no fix yet.

Notes on the retrieval paper before I forget the argument, because I want to bring it to the reading group on Wednesday and I always lose the thread if I leave it a day. The claim is that their gain comes from the reranker and not from the retriever, and the ablation they show does support that, but only in the setting where the corpus is small enough that recall at a hundred is already above ninety. On the larger corpus the reranker cannot rescue what the first stage never returned, and they say this themselves in a footnote rather than in the results section, which I think is a choice. The second thing I want to raise is the training data. They fine tune on a hard negative set mined with the same retriever they are evaluating, so the negatives are exactly the documents that retriever finds confusing, and that is a closed loop. It does not make the numbers wrong but it makes them specific to that first stage, and nobody reading the abstract would know. The third thing is the latency table, which is measured on a single query at a time with a warm cache, and that is not how anybody serves this, because batching changes the picture completely and the reranker is the part that batches badly. I ran their code on our own index last night with the checkpoint they released and I got about two points lower on the same metric, which is close enough that I believe the headline number. What I still cannot reproduce is speedup they claim for the cascaded version.

Right, writing this down while I still remember the shape of it, because the postmortem is on Monday and I do not trust myself to reconstruct the order later. The symptom was that requests to the pricing service started timing out at about twenty past nine, but only the ones that came through the mobile gateway, which is why the dashboards looked fine for the first quarter of an hour. The pool on the pricing side has thirty connections and the mobile gateway holds a request open while it waits on a second call downstream, so thirty slow mobile requests are enough to starve every other caller on the box. That is not a new fact about the system, it is written in the runbook, and we still walked into it. What was new is why the downstream call got slow, and that turns out to be a migration somebody ran on the currency table at nine fifteen, which took a lock for about four minutes. Four minutes of a held lock on a table that every pricing lookup reads is enough to fill the pool, and once the pool is full the retries make it worse, because our client retries three times with no backoff at all. I have checked and the retry policy has been like that since the service was written, so this was always going to happen the first time anything downstream got slow. The fix I want to argue for is a separate pool for the mobile path and a real backoff on the client.

Thinking through the momentum sleeve before the risk meeting, and I want to be blunt about what the backtest does and does not show. The signal is twelve month total return skipping the most recent month, ranked inside sector, and rebalanced monthly with a five day execution window rather than a single close, because we cannot pretend we trade at the close on the same tick everybody else does. On that construction the sleeve returns about seven per cent a year gross with a drawdown of nineteen in the worst stretch, which was March of that first year. Net of the cost model it is closer to four and a half, and the cost model is the part I trust least, because it uses average spread rather than the spread we actually pay in size on the smaller names. Half of the gross return comes from the short leg, and the short leg is where borrow gets expensive exactly when the signal is strongest, so I would rather quote the long only version and treat the rest as an upside case. The other thing the committee should hear is that the whole result rests on the sector neutralisation. Without it the sleeve is a bet on two sectors and the drawdown doubles, which tells you the alpha is inside the sector and not across them. I have run it on the second half only and it holds, weaker but the same sign, and I have run it on the first half only and it is stronger, which is the ordering you expect if the effect is decaying. I am not putting capital behind it until it survives a proper out of simple test.

Right, this is the focaccia written down because I am tired of explaining it to whoever is on mornings, and every time I explain it I say it slightly differently and then I get annoyed when it comes out slightly differently. The dough is not the hard part. The hard part is that the dough wants more time than the rota gives it, and everybody tries to fix that with more yeast, and more yeast is why the last three trays tasted of beer. So the first thing to understand is that we make it the night before, always, and if somebody has not made it the night before then we do not have focaccia that day and we put something else on the board. That is not me being difficult, it is that a four hour focaccia is a different bread and the people who come back for it will notice. The flour is the strong one in the paper sack and not the tipo zero zero, and the water is more than you think, about eighty five percent, so the dough will look wrong in the mixer and you have to trust it. Oil in the tray, oil on your hands, oil on top before it goes in, and do not be careful with it. The salt on top is the course one and not the fine one, because fine salt dissolves and you taste nothing, and it goes on after the second prove and never before, since salt on the surface pulls the water out and the top goes leathery. Now the order for the morning person. First take the tray out of the fridge and leave it somewhere warm for two hours. Second dimple it with your fingers all the way down to the bottom of the tray. Third put the rosemary and the salt on and give it another twenty minutes. Fourth put it in at two forty for eighteen minutes and turn the tray once. That is the whole thing, and the only part that changes is the oven, because the one at the back runs hot and wants two thirty. The other thing that goes wrong is the tomato version. If you are doing the tomato one the tomatoes goes on before the second prove and not after, otherwise they sit on top and burn before the bread underneath is done, and half the tray comes out with black skins on it. The cherry tomatoes from the market are better than the tinned for this and they cost less in season, so use them while we can. And whoever is on mornings should check the yeast on a Monday, because we had a week where nothing rose properly and it turned out the yeast had been open since before I went away, and nobody thought to look at it because the tub was still half full. The last thing is that it goes on the board as focaccia and not as flat bread. I have seen it written up as flat bread twice and it is not the same thing, and the person who wrote it that way knows who they are. If we run out by two then write it off the board rather than making a second batch in a hurry, because the hurried one is the one people remember.

Right, this is the handover for the ingestion service and I am dictating it rather than writing it because I leave on Friday and the doc I started is four bullet points and a diagram nobody understands. Start with what the service actually does, because the name is wrong. It is called ingestion and it does two unrelated things. It pulls files from partner buckets on a schedule, and it also serves a synchronous endpoint that partners push to when they cannot be bothered with a bucket. Those two paths share almost no code and they fail for completely different reasons, and if you only remember one thing from this handover remember that, because every time somebody says ingestion is broken the first question is which half. The pull path is the one that pages you. It runs every fifteen minutes, it keeps a cursor per partner in the state table, and the cursor is the thing that goes wrong. If a partner reuploads a file with an older modified time the cursor skips it forever, and the only way to notice is that their row count is flat while everybody else moves. There is a query in the runbook for that and it is the single most useful query in the whole repo. The push path is the one that generates support tickets. Partners send us CSV and about a third of them send us CSV that is technically valid and practically horrible. The two failures you will see constantly are a new line inside a quoted description field, which is legal and which our parser handles fine, and a comma inside an unquoted address field, which is not legal and which nothing can handle. When a partner complains that their upload is broken it is almost always the second one, and the polite way to tell them is to send them the row number and let them look at it themselves. Do not offer to fix their file. We did that once and it became a standing expectation for two years. On the code, the part that will surprise you is the retry wrapper. It looks like it retries the whole request and it does not, it retries the parse only, and that is deliberate, because retrying the request duplicates rows and there is no idempotency key on the partner side. There is a comment saying that. The comment is wrong about why but right about what. On the things I have not finished, the biggest one is that the schema validation is per file and it should be per partner, because two partners legitimately disagree about whether a blank means zero or unknown and we currently resolve that with an if statement in the middle of the parser. It works. It is embarrassing. I would not touch it in your first month. And the last thing, the alert on parse failure rate is set at five per cent and it should be per partner too, because one partner having a bad day looks the same as everybody having a slightly bad day and those need different responses.

That gap is the actual finding. Everything else in this write up is detail. What expired was the intermediate on the internal mesh, not the public certificate, which is why the status page stayed green and why the first three people to look at it concluded there was nothing wrong. Internal traffic between the two payment services failed closed, which is correct behaviour, and the retry logic in front of it kept the error rate under the alert threshold for the first half hour by spreading the failures out. So the alert threshold hid it, the retries hid it, and the status page hid it, and all three of those are things we chose. On the certificate itself, the renewal job had been failing for nine days. It failed silently because it writes its result to a log stream nobody reads and it exits zero regardless. The reason it was failing is that the hostname in the mesh config gained a trailing dot in a change three weeks ago, which is legal and which the mesh accepts, but the certificate authority client compares the requested name against its own record as a plain string and the dot made it a mismatch. So the request was rejected every night, and every night the job said nothing. I want to be careful here because there are two separate mistakes and only one of them is interesting. The uninteresting one is that somebody added a dot. That is fine, it is a correct configuration, and I would not ask anybody to stop doing it. The interesting one is that a job whose entire purpose is to prevent an outage can fail for nine days without anybody knowing. Recovery took thirty one minutes from the point somebody looked at the right log, and twenty of those thirty one were spent finding who had permission to run the renewal by hand. That is the second finding. On follow ups, I have opened three tickets and I am going to describe them rather than list them because they are not equally important. The one that matters is alerting on the age of the certificate rather than on the job exiting non zero, because the job exits zero when it fails. The second is the permission thing, which is a five minute change and a two week conversation. The third is that the internal mesh should have its own status signal, and I am least confident about that one because it is the kind of thing that gets built and then ignored. The roll back plan we did not need but should write down anyway is that the mesh can run in permissive mode for about an hour before the compliance people notice, and that is worth knowing at three in the morning.

Right, this is the draft of the troubleshooting page for the log agent and I am dictating it so I can hear whether the ordering makes sense before I write it properly. Start with the symptom the reader actually has, not with the architecture, because nobody arrives at a troubleshooting page wanting to learn how the agent works. The symptom is almost always the same, which is that events appear in the console with the wrong timestamp or they appear split across several entries. The split case is the one people misdiagnose. What has happened is that the application wrote a multi line message and the agent read each physical line as a separate event, because by default the agent has no idea that a stack trace is one thing. So the fix is the multiline pattern in the agent config, and the pattern has to match the first line of the event rather than the continuation, which is the opposite of what most people try first, new paragraph. I want to say that twice in the page because it is the single most common mistake. If your application writes a line break inside a JSON field the same thing happens for a different reason, and the fix there is not a multiline pattern at all, it is telling the agent the input is JSON so it stops treating physical lines as boundaries. Those two look identical in the console and they need different fixes, so the page needs a way for the reader to tell them apart quickly. The quickest test I know is whether the first fragment is valid JSON on its own. If it is, you have the multiline problem. If it is not, you have the JSON problem. On the timestamp case, there are three causes and I want them in this order because that is the order of likelihood and not the order of interest. The first is that the agent is parsing the timestamp with the wrong format string and falling back to ingestion time, which looks like every event arriving at once. The second is a genuine clock problem on the host, which is rare now but still happens on the older virtual machines. The third is that somebody has two agents running on the same file, which produces duplicates with slightly different times and is by far the most confusing to look at. I have seen the third one three times and every time it took a day. On the structure of the page, I do not want a decision tree diagram. We tried that on the networking page and the feedback was that people cannot find themselves in it. What works better is a short list of symptoms at the top with anchors, and then a section per symptom that says what you will see, what causes it, and what to change, in that order, every time. Consistency matters more than cleverness here. The last thing, and this is a note to myself rather than to the page, is that the config examples need to be tested before they go in. The examples on the current page do not parse. Two of them have the wrong indentation and one refers to an option that was renamed a year ago, and every one of those got there because somebody wrote an example from memory and nobody ran it.

So these are my notes for the referee report on the manuscript about the survey instrument, and I am dictating them because I think more clearly out loud and because the report is due Thursday. That is not nothing and it is also not what the claim requires. The authors know this. There is a sentence in the discussion that almost says it. What is missing is any analysis at the level of the individual case, and the data to do it are clearly in hand. The second problem is the reporting of the item statistics. I have flagged it as a required correction rather than a criticism. The third problem is a real one and I am not sure the authors can fix it within a revision. The sample is a convenience sample from two institutions and the paper describes it as representative of the sector. It is not, and the two institutions differ from the sector on the one variable that the instrument is most sensitive to. I would ask them to either drop the representativeness claim entirely or add a second sample, and I expect they will drop the claim, which is the honest outcome. There is also a smaller thing in the data appendix that I want to mention because it will bite whoever tries to replicate this. The supplementary file is comma separated and three of the free text response fields contain a comma without quoting, so the file does not parse in any standard reader and the column count varies by row. I only found the real values by opening it in a text editor. That should be fixed before publication regardless of what happens to the rest of the paper. On the writing I have very little to say. The paper is clear, the notation is consistent, and the literature review is fair to the work it disagrees with, which is rarer than it should be.

Writing up the flaky test properly because I have now been asked about it three times. The test is not flaky in the way people mean when they say flaky. It fails about one run in nine and it fails for a reason, which is that it asserts on the order of two rows that come back from a query with no order by clause. On the developer machines the planner picks a sequential scan and the rows come back in insertion order every time, so it passes locally forever. On the build machine the table is larger because the seed job runs twice, the planner picks the index, and the order changes. That is the whole mechanism and there is nothing intermittent about it. I have not fixed it yet and I want to say why. The obvious fix is to add an order by to the query inside the test, which makes the test pass and hides the fact that the production code also depends on that order in one place, in the export path, where it has never been noticed because the export is small. So the fix is in the production query, not in the test, and then the test can keep asserting on order because the order will be real. I have opened a separate ticket for the seed job running twice, since that is a build configuration problem rather than a test problem and it is also why the build machine has been slowing down since June. None of this is urgent this week, but I would rather nobody quarantined the test in the meantime, because a quarantined test is how this stops being anybody's problem.

Right, this is for the group that arrives on Sunday and honestly it is more of a warning than a briefing, so send it as it is, do not make it sound like a brochure. The trek is not hard. I want to be clear about that first because people arrive terrified after reading the internet. It is eleven days of walking uphill slowly, and slowly is the whole trick, and the people who struggle are almost never the unfit ones, they are the fit ones who go too fast on day two because they feel great. If you feel great on day two you are going too fast. The bit nobody warns you about is not the altitude, it is the food and the boredom. You will eat the same three things for eleven days and by day six you will have strong opinions about garlic soup. Bring something that tastes of home, a stupid amount of it, and be generous with it, because the person who shares snacks on day seven becomes everybody's favourite human. Bring a book you actually want to read, not a book you think you should read on a mountain, because there is nothing to do after six in the evening and the electricity is a rumour. The other real thing is the money. Bring cash, more than you think, in small notes, because the machines at the bottom do not work half the time and the machines further up do not exist. Everything gets more expensive the higher you go for the extremely good reason that somebody carried it there on their back. Do not haggle about that. Haggle about nothing, actually, at least not with anybody carrying a load. The kit list is the same as it has always been and I am not repeating it, but two things get ignored every single group. One is that your boots need to have been worn before you get on the plane, and worn means walked in, not tried on. Every trip somebody arrives with boots so new they squeak and by day three they cannot put their heels down. The other is the sleeping bag rating. You will be warm in the day and genuinely cold at four in the morning at the top two lodges, and no amount of enthusiasm fixes a thin bag. Rent a better one in town, it costs about the same as two coffees at home. On the altitude, we go slowly, we take the acclimatisation day even if everybody feels brilliant, and nobody gets to be brave about a headache. Tell me about a headache. Tell me about it early, tell me about it even if you think it is nothing, and I will almost always tell you it is nothing, and the one time it is not nothing is the reason I ask. That is the only rule I will be strict about the entire eleven days. Everything else, wear what you like, walk how you like, take four hundred photographs of the same mountain like everybody does, and do not apologise for being slow because slow is correct.

This change is in the retry layer and it is bigger than I wanted it to be, which I will explain, because the original bug was tiny and the fix kept pulling on things.

The reported problem was that uploads over about 40 MB failed roughly one time in nine on mobile networks and the failure looked like a success in our logs, which is why it took three weeks for anyone to notice.

What actually happens is that the client streams the file in 4 MB chunks, and if a chunk times out the client retries it, and the retry uses a fresh signed URL, but the server was keying the assembly by URL rather than by upload id, so the retried chunk landed in a second half finished assembly and the first one was never cleaned up. Then the finaliser saw a complete set of chunks for the wrong assembly, returned 200, and we stored a file that was missing about 8 MB out of the middle.

The reason it looked fine is that our checksum was computed client side before the upload and stored alongside it, and nobody was comparing it to anything on the way back out.

There are really three changes in here.

1. Keying is now on upload id and the signed URL is just a credential, which is a nine line change and is the actual bug fix.
2. The finaliser verifies the assembled length against the declared length before it returns, and refuses with a 409 if they differ, which is another twenty lines and is the thing that would have caught this in week one.
3. I added a stored checksum comparison on read, behind a flag, defaulting off, because I do not know what it costs on the big files and I did not want to find out in production on a Friday. I have it running on the staging bucket with the flag on and the read path is about 4 per cent slower on a 200 MB object and unmeasurably different under 10 MB, but staging has one client and production has forty thousand so I do not trust that number very far.

Testing:
*   I wrote a test that uploads six chunks, kills the third one twice, and asserts the assembled length.
*   I wrote a second test that asserts the finaliser returns 409 when a chunk is missing entirely rather than 200.
*   I wrote a third test that runs the whole flow with the read checksum flag on and off and asserts identical bytes out.
*   All three fail on the old code and pass on the new code, which I checked by stashing the fix rather than by trusting myself.

What I did not test is the concurrent case where two clients upload the same upload id, because I could not make that happen without writing a fake client and I ran out of appetite, and I think it is genuinely unlikely given the id comes from a server side create call, but it is not impossible and somebody should say so in review.

There is also a migration question I have not solved. Any file already stored with a short assembly is still short, and this change does not find them or fix them. I can write a job that walks the bucket and compares stored length to declared length, and on the numbers I have that is about 2.1 million objects and maybe six hours, but I would rather do that as a separate change with its own review than bolt it onto this one.

The logging is different too, and I should flag that because it will show up in dashboards. The old code logged an assembly complete line per URL, so a retried upload logged twice and our success count was inflated by however many retries happened, which is why the graph looked healthy. Now it logs once per upload id, so the absolute number of successes will appear to drop by something like 3 per cent overnight without anything getting worse. Somebody will ask about that on Monday and the answer is that the old number was wrong.

Deployment is safe in either order because the new keying is backwards compatible with in flight uploads, or I believe it is, and the reason I believe it is that the URL is still accepted and ignored rather than rejected. I would deploy the server first, watch the 409 rate for an hour, and then turn the read flag on for internal accounts only. If the 409 rate is anything other than near zero then we have a second bug and I want to know before the flag goes anywhere near a customer.

The cold chain is the part that keeps me awake. The vaccine carrier holds four ice packs and the packs come from the health post freezer, and the freezer at the health post has been reliable since it was replaced in Poush but it is on the same line as the pump, so if the pump runs at night the freezer competes with it. The cold chain is the part that keeps me awake because everything else in this plan can slip by a day without harming anybody. Site by site, Tuesday is the school ground at Chapagaun from nine until two, and we expect around 45 children based on the ward register, which lists 51 but four of those families have moved and two are recorded twice. The team is Kamala, who is the auxiliary nurse midwife and is the only person who can actually administer, myself for the register and the crowd, and one female community health volunteer per site who is different at each site and who needs to be told the day before, not on the morning. Supplies are 200 doses, 260 syringes because we always break some, four safety boxes, two carriers, eight ice packs, the paper registers, and the tally sheets which I have printed 30 of. The consumables order number is CH-2214-B and the reference for the carrier loan from the district store is DS/0417. The tally sheet template is on the shared drive under health/round4/tally_v3.xlsx and the reporting portal is at https://reporting.example.gov.np/immunisation, and the login is the ward one, not mine, which caught us out last time. Money is 8,400 rupees for the volunteer allowances at 400 a day per site, plus fuel for the motorcycle on the two long days, plus 1,200 for the tea and biscuits at the market day site which is not an official line and which I will put through as refreshments as usual. The risks, and I want these written down so that nobody is surprised, are the freezer sharing the line with the pump, the road above the second bend if it rains, Kamala being the only administrator so that any illness on her side stops the round entirely, and the register being wrong in both directions so that our denominator is soft. If the road closes we do the settlements from the upper side on foot from the ridge, which adds an hour each way and means an early start rather than a cancelled day. If the freezer fails we borrow from the private clinic at the bazaar, which the owner has agreed to informally and which I have not put in writing anywhere. If Kamala is ill we stop, and we do not attempt to be clever about it. One last thing, the registers themselves go into the cupboard in the ward office at the end of each day and not into anybody's bag, because we lost a day of entries in Ashoj that way and I do not want to explain that to the district a second time.

House notes for the two weeks we are away, and I am going to be thorough because last time I left a list of five things and you rang me four times. The boiler needs the pressure to sit between one and one and a half on the dial, and if it drops below one it will lock out and show a red light, and the fix is the small grey tap underneath which you open a quarter turn until the needle comes back and then close firmly. Do not leave that tap open. If the boiler locks out twice in a day then something else is wrong and the number for the engineer is on the fridge. The water is fine to drink from the kitchen tap but the bathroom one runs from the tank, so use the kitchen for the kettle. Bin day is Thursday, and the bins go out on Wednesday night because the truck comes at about half six and has never once come later. The recycling is fortnightly and this fortnight is the one where it does go out, so both bins on the first Wednesday and only the black one on the second. Thursday for the bins, and please do not leave them out afterwards because the wind takes them down the lane. The heating timer is set for six until eight in the morning and five until ten at night, which is more than you will need if the weather stays as it is, and the dial is the round one on the wall in the hall, and turning it clockwise is warmer even though the arrow suggests otherwise. The plants in the front room need water twice a week and the one in the kitchen window needs it every other day because the radiator underneath it dries it out. The one on the landing needs nothing at all and will die if you water it, which I say every time and which somebody always ignores. The post will pile up and most of it can go straight in the recycling, but anything from the council or anything that looks like a bill should go on the shelf by the stairs rather than being opened, and if anything arrives that needs signing then just refuse it and they will leave a card. The neighbours are Nirmala on the left, who is in most days and who has our number, and the couple on the right who we do not really know and who park across the entrance sometimes. If you need the drive then knocking works, and being annoyed about it does not, which took me two years to learn. The internet router is behind the television and the password is on the underside of it on a sticker, and if it stops working the fix is to unplug it for a full minute rather than the ten seconds everyone tries first. The television needs the grey remote for the volume and the black one for everything else, and there is no combination in which one remote does both, and I have stopped trying. The car is staying on the drive and is taxed until the end of next month, and it will start if you turn it over for a moment first, and if you need to move it the keys are in the drawer under the kettle. Rubbish that is not bin rubbish, meaning the broken chair and the box of tiles, is going to the tip when we are back and can sit in the shed until then. If the freezer alarm goes off, and it does sometimes for no reason, the reset is the button on the front panel held for three seconds, and if it goes off twice then look at whether the door is sitting properly on the seal because the top drawer sticks out if it is overfilled. Finally, the thing I actually worry about, which is the leak under the kitchen sink. It is not leaking now and it has not leaked since it was fixed in the spring, but there is a towel under there and if the towel is wet then turn the water off at the stopcock, which is in the same cupboard at the back on the left, and then ring the plumber whose card is with the engineer's on the fridge. The spare key is with Nirmala next door. She knows we are away and she knows roughly when we are back, and if anything happens that is not on this list then she is a better first call than either of us because she will actually be standing in the house.

Okay, this is everything I know about the tender for the community hall roof, and I am putting it in one message because three people have now asked me the same questions in a slightly different order. The notice went up on the fourteenth and the closing date is the twenty eighth at four in the afternoon, which is a Friday, and the office shuts at five so there is no argument to be had about arriving at ten past. The work is the full roof on the old hall, which is the one behind the water tank and not the newer building that everyone assumes, and if you are looking at the drawing then it is the structure marked with a dot on the north west corner, because that dot is how they distinguish the two on every sheet in the file. The scope as written is stripping the existing sheets, replacing the purlins where they are rotten, which is most of them on the north side, laying new sheets, and making good the parapet where the old fixings have pulled through. There is a line in the scope about guttering that is ambiguous, because it says make good existing guttering and the existing guttering is not really there any more, so I would price for replacement and say clearly in the covering note that you have done so, rather than pricing for nothing and arguing about it later. The bid documents cost 2,000 rupees and you collect them from the ward office in person between ten and one, and they will not send them, and they will not accept a photograph of a receipt, and yes somebody has tried. Bring the firm's registration and the VAT certificate and a copy of the last tax clearance, and bring two copies of each because the clerk keeps one. The bid security is 5 per cent of your quoted amount and it has to be a bank guarantee valid for ninety days from the closing date, not a cheque, and the ninety days catches people out because most of the standard forms come out at sixty. If you need to ask them anything formally then write to tenders dot office at kavre municipality dot gov dot np and copy the ward secretary, and expect three working days for a reply, and do not rely on the phone number in the notice because it rings in a room nobody sits in. Anything they tell you verbally is worth nothing at the evaluation, so if a clarification matters, get it in writing or price around it. On the evaluation itself, it is lowest evaluated bid rather than lowest bid, which in practice with this office has meant that they do look at the technical submission and they do disqualify on missing documents, and last year two of the five bidders were thrown out on paperwork before any prices were opened. So the boring part is the part that decides it. The technical submission wants three similar works in the last five years with completion certificates, and similar has been read generously here before, so a school roof counts, and a shed does not. It wants the site engineer's licence and a signed statement that the engineer will be present, and they have asked for that engineer by name on site during a visit, so do not put down somebody who is in another district all week. On the price, the quantities in the bill are measured from the drawing and the drawing is from 2009, and the roof has been patched twice since, so the sheet count is low by my estimate by about 8 per cent and the purlin count is low by more than that. You are bidding on their quantities, so the honest way to handle it is to price their quantities and flag the variance in the covering note, because raising it after award is a fight you lose slowly. There is a site visit on the twentieth at eleven, and it is not mandatory but the people who skip it are the people who get the purlin count wrong, and the caretaker will open the ceiling hatch if you ask him nicely and bring your own torch. Take photographs of the north side from inside, because that is the evidence you will want if there is a variation claim later. Payment terms are 30 per cent on mobilisation against a guarantee, 50 per cent on progress certified by their engineer, and the rest on final measurement, and the final 20 per cent has historically taken four to five months to arrive, so please price your cash flow honestly rather than pretending that money comes in October. The retention is 5 per cent held for a year. My overall read is that it is a reasonable job at a fair size for a small firm, the office is slow but not difficult, and the two ways people lose it here are missing documents and the guttering line, and both of those are free to get right.
